claims.text: An MTP-based perturbation scheme can efficiently compute free-energy differences in Ta-based refractory BCC high-entropy alloys.
Including liquid-phase configurations in the MTP training set avoids extrapolation artifacts.
Including chemical short-range-order states in the MTP training set avoids extrapolation artifacts.
Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 is an example of the targeted Ta-based refractory BCC solid-solution alloy.
The relevant solid and liquid phases can be studied near melting at 1500–2500 K and zero pressure.
MTPs construct contracted rotationally invariant descriptors of each atom's local environment.
MTP moment tensors encode radial, angular, and chemical-species information about local atomic environments.
MTP descriptors accurately represent complex multicomponent liquid structure and chemical short-range order.
An MTP builds a polynomially regressed relationship between its descriptors and the potential-energy surface.
MTP evaluation of perturbed configurations is sufficiently efficient to avoid the expensive sampling required by ab initio thermodynamic integration.
When configurations remain inside the MTP training manifold, statistical reweighting can estimate the required free-energy differences.
The proposed scheme will reproduce ab initio solid-liquid free-energy differences within 5%.
The proposed scheme will reduce computational cost by a factor of 10–100.
Standard DFT-based ab initio thermodynamic integration is prohibitively expensive because it requires extensive phase-space sampling.
EAM potentials fail to capture complex liquid structure in multicomponent systems.
The approach is valid only when the MTP training set contains representative liquid and short-range-order configurations.
Applying the MTP to unexplored compositions or extreme temperatures outside its training manifold will produce artifacts.
Training-set gaps in liquid and short-range-order configurations can cause extrapolation errors and control the accuracy of the perturbation scheme.

A greater than 10% deviation after excluding liquid and short-range-order training configurations would establish that training coverage is critical and that the apparent efficiency gain is an extrapolation artifact.
